summary: Defines a bidirectional mapping for group chat between SIP users and XMPP users, mapping MSRP-based chat to XMPP Multi-User Chat so the two can talk to each other.

eli5.summary: This is a translator so people on two different chat systems can sit in the same room.

questions: how do sip and xmpp group chat interwork
what is the msrp to muc mapping
what is a sip to xmpp gateway
how does an msrp nickname map to xmpp
subtitle: How a SIP/MSRP group chat and an XMPP chat room can be bridged so users of either side can talk in the same room.

tldr.problem: SIP and XMPP can both run multi-party text chat, but they model it differently, so users on one side cannot join a room on the other.
tldr.mechanism: Gateways translate between XMPP Multi-User Chat (MUC) and MSRP-based SIP chat, mapping actions such as entering a room, setting a nickname, sending messages, inviting users and leaving.
tldr.outcome: It covers only a basic subset of groupchat features. Room administration, moderation and end-to-end encryption for multi-party chat are left out.

today: RFC 7702 is a Proposed Standard from December 2015, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7247 and RFC 7701.

sections.title: What the Document Maps
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) can both be used for multi-party text chat, often called groupchat. To let the two worlds interwork, RFC 7702 defines a bidirectional protocol mapping between SIP-based chat using the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) and the XMPP Multi-User Chat (MUC) extension. The shared architecture, address mapping and error handling come from RFC 7247, and the MSRP chat extensions it maps come from RFC 7701.

Both MUC and MSRP have many features, such as kicking out and banning users, changing the room subject, moderation and destroying a room. The RFC covers only a basic subset: joining a room, setting or changing a nickname (without permanently registering it), changing presence, sending a message to everyone, sending a private message, inviting another user and leaving. The readers it targets are developers who already run a system on one technology and want to reach the other.
sections.eli5: Two chat apps each have their own way to run a clubhouse. This document says how to carry the basic things, like walking in, talking and leaving, from one clubhouse to the other.

sections.title: Architectural Assumptions
sections.content:
XMPP and MSRP differ in how they treat groupchat. In XMPP, a message of type groupchat is just another stanza, handled by the XMPP server or a multi-user chat component. In MSRP, a chat session is a kind of media, like audio or video. A conference focus handles the SIP signaling to set up, manage and end the session, while a separate entity called an MSRP switch carries the session data. How the focus and the switch talk to each other is left to the implementation.

The RFC names the logical pieces: a SIP proxy with a SIP-to-XMPP gateway (S2X), a SIP conference focus and MSRP switch with an MSRP-to-XMPP gateway (M2X), and on the XMPP side a server with XMPP-to-SIP (X2S) and XMPP-to-MSRP (X2M) gateways plus a MUC service. These are logical entities and several can be co-located. The RFC notes that an XMPP service would likely use a single gateway rather than separate ones for SIP and MSRP.

The user does not have to use a home SIP proxy to reach an XMPP room. The document shows the expected path for simplicity, and says nothing in it discourages other deployment layouts.
sections.eli5: One part of the system is the front desk that sets up the room, and another part is the mail carrier that moves the messages. The translators stand between those parts and the other chat system.

sections.title: From XMPP MUC to MSRP
sections.content:
To enter a room, an XMPP user sends a directed presence stanza to the room address, with her chosen nickname as the resourcepart and an empty x element in the MUC namespace. The XMPP server hands it to the XMPP-to-SIP gateway, which turns it into a SIP INVITE whose SDP offer describes an MSRP session. The conference focus accepts with a 200 OK that includes the isfocus feature tag and the switch's MSRP address, and the gateway sends an ACK. The gateway MUST map the bare JID of the XMPP sender to the SIP From header and carry the resourcepart as the GRUU portion of the SIP URI.

Next the gateway sets the nickname with an MSRP NICKNAME request using the Use-Nickname header, and subscribes to the conference event package so the user can receive presence for the existing occupants. The focus returns a NOTIFY with the participant list, which the gateway translates into a series of XMPP presence stanzas, plus a separate message if a subject is included.

A message to all occupants is a stanza of type groupchat sent to the room, and the gateway maps it to an MSRP SEND. Because XMPP expects the sender to receive a reflected copy of its own message, the gateway reflects it back. A private message is type chat sent to the occupant's room JID; a gateway that supports it MUST add private-messages to the a=chatroom SDP attribute.

A nickname change is another presence stanza. If the switch finds the nickname is taken, it answers 425, and the gateway returns an XMPP presence error with a conflict condition, or may retry with a new nickname itself. Invitations (mediated ones only) become a SIP REFER to the focus, tracked by NOTIFY. Leaving is a presence stanza of type unavailable, which the gateway turns into a SIP BYE.
sections.eli5: When Juliet walks into the room, the translator fills out the SIP paperwork for her, picks her name tag and brings back the list of who is inside. Anything she says goes out through the translator, and she gets a copy back too.

sections.title: From MSRP to XMPP MUC
sections.content:
In the other direction, the SIP user sends an INVITE with an SDP offer containing an MSRP media line, mandatory path and chatroom attributes, and an accept-types attribute for the Message/CPIM wrapper. The SIP proxy hands the request to its SIP-to-XMPP gateway. The gateway MAY wait for an MSRP NICKNAME chunk before joining the MUC room, or MAY use a temporary nickname such as the SIP From display name. It also takes part in the conference event subscription, then sends presence from the SIP user to the MUC room.

The MUC service replies with presence from every existing occupant. XMPP sends the room roster as many presence stanzas, while SIP uses one conference information document. So the gateway has to track the user's own in-room presence, which per XEP-0045 is the last presence stanza in the initial batch, and only then build the full participant list. If the presence arrives before the SIP subscription exists, the server SHOULD cache the list.

A public message is an MSRP SEND to the room. The gateway translates it to an XMPP message and SHOULD wait for the reflected copy from the MUC room before replying 200 OK to the sender. A nickname change is a new NICKNAME request; an XMPP conflict error becomes MSRP code 425. An invitation is a SIP REFER, and since progress cannot be known until the invitee joins, implementations are advised to end the REFER subscription after the first NOTIFY with 100 Trying. A SIP BYE becomes an unavailable presence stanza.
sections.eli5: Romeo asks the translator to get him into the XMPP clubhouse. The translator shows up with a name for him, collects the guest list into one sheet for him, and passes his messages along.

sections.title: Nicknames and Display Names
sections.content:
A nickname is the unique identifier of a participant within a room, while a display name is a friendly label that need not be unique. Implementations SHOULD apply the string preparation and comparison rules for nicknames from RFC 7700.

In the SIP conference event package, the nickname is the XCON nickname attribute of the user element and the display name is the display-text element. In XMPP, the nickname is the resourcepart of the occupant JID and the display name is the nick element. In practice display-text is treated as canonical in SIP, and nick is rarely used in XMPP. So for display, SIP implementations ought to use display-text when no XCON nickname is present, and XMPP implementations ought to use the resourcepart when no nick is present.

If a SIP nickname and an XMPP nickname conflict, the gateway is responsible for adjusting the nickname and telling the client which unique nickname was used. Separately, the RFC warns that MSRP messages can exceed the size an XMPP service allows; RFC 7573 discusses that issue.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the room needs a different name tag. If two people pick the same one, the translator changes one and tells that person what the new tag says.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the SIP, MSRP, XMPP, RFC 7247, RFC 7701 and MUC specifications all apply. A gateway MUST meet the minimum security requirements of the protocols it translates between. Adding gateways does introduce new risks. End-to-end confidentiality and integrity between user agents on either side of an MSRP-to-XMPP gateway are possible only if common formats are supported, and for multi-party messaging the RFC says that problem has not been solved in a standardized way.

Features left out of the baseline, such as administering rooms, kicking and banning users and moderation, are relevant to security. Users who need them cannot get them through a gateway in a standardized manner and must use a native MSRP or XMPP client. The RFC also notes that there is no widely deployed method for end-to-end encryption of multi-party instant messages, so it makes no recommendation on that.
sections.eli5: The translator can read what passes through it, and nobody has a standard way yet to keep a group chat secret from it. Rules like banning people also do not cross the bridge.
